Hormuz vessel traffic falls to nine as crude flows reach 33.7 million barrels
Despite the decline in vessel traffic, crude oil flows out of the Strait of Hormuz reached 33.7 million barrels in the week beginning September 20, preliminary Kpler data showed on September 25. The volume puts exports roughly on track with the previous week’s levels.
The traffic so far this week involved 19 tankers, including 17 very large crude carriers (VLCCs), which can each carry about 2 million barrels of oil. Most of the tankers were carrying crude from Saudi Arabia, followed by Iraq.
For the full previous week, 49.2 million barrels of crude were shipped out through Hormuz, according to Kpler.
On September 23, about 60 commercial vessels of all types transited the Strait of Hormuz, carrying the highest daily volume of crude oil since early July, a US official said on condition of anonymity.
Saudi Aramco has increased its exports through Hormuz after attacks on its East-West Pipeline earlier this month halted shipments from the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
Before the Iran war began on February 28, the Strait of Hormuz typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day, including tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers and container ships, accounting for about 20% of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies.

The Defense Department on Monday announced framework agreements with Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin aimed at expanding production of critical Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, interceptor components as the military seeks to replenish missile inventories through expanded, long-term production capacity.
The agreements come as demand for Patriot and THAAD interceptors has increased following conflicts in Iran and Ukraine that strained U.S. missile inventories .
They also come days after a Center for Strategic and International Studies analysis estimated the United States had depleted roughly two-thirds of its pre-war Patriot interceptor inventory during the conflict with Iran.
Defense officials said the agreements are intended to support the department’s long-term procurement objective of nearly 14,000 Patriot and THAAD interceptors by providing sustained demand signals to critical suppliers throughout the defense industrial base.
The initiative is designed to triple production capacity for Patriot Advanced Capability-3, or PAC-3, Missile Segment Enhancement interceptors and quadruple production capacity for THAAD interceptors.
“Building the Arsenal of Freedom requires robust, dynamic supply chains at every level of the industrial base,” Michael P. Duffey, under secretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, said in a statement.

"Regulatory uncertainty heightens permitting and completion risk for new-build projects, especially if they have not secured required permits by financial close. Limited grid capacity will encourage more data center developers to pursue behind-the-meter (BTM) or co-located arrangements with generation assets," it said.
Fitch believes power supply challenges will spur developers to consider incorporating BTM solutions in new data center financings.
While typical BTM components, including turbines, reciprocating engines and battery energy storage systems, "have established operating track records, they have limited demonstrated history operating in islanded configurations that serve highly variable high-performance computing and AI workloads," the rating agency said.
Sufficient pipeline capacity and contracted gas transportation and supply help mitigate fuel supply risks for the BTM system, it noted.
"Gas cost pass-through mechanisms are typically indexed to a contractual heat rate, which leaves the project exposed to residual risk if it operates less efficiently.
Co-located or BTM supply supported by long-term contracts "with highly creditworthy counterparties, particularly with take-or-pay contract structures, is viewed as a stronger characteristic for merchant generators supplying power to data centers."

(Bloomberg) —
The Trump administration is imposing tariffs of as much as 100% on imported drones and their components, escalating efforts to reduce US reliance on foreign suppliers and potentially accelerating a decoupling of drone supply chains with China.
“In the long term, we’re probably slipping towards an outcome of a hard decoupling for at least certain types of drones,” said Christopher Beddor, deputy China research director at Gavekal Dragonomics.
US restrictions on new foreign-made models last year have curbed Chinese access to the American market, while Beijing has tightened scrutiny of drone-related exports to the US. Chinese drone exports to the US fell to about $50 million in the first half of this year, roughly half the level recorded a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data.
The drone duties rely instead on Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which requires an investigation before allowing import restrictions on national security grounds. Trump has invoked the same power to collect tariffs on goods including steel and aluminum, semi-finished copper, and cars and auto parts.
Probes into robotics and wind turbines are ongoing under 232 authority.
Smaller drones lacking capabilities deemed especially sensitive for national security will face a 25% duty, as will other components.

Key Facts

The US Army selected five companies on August 26 to build nuclear microreactors at five installations. The agreements are worth up to $2.2 billion through fiscal 2031. The program is called Janus.
Fuel choices differ across the group. Radiant and Antares plan to use HALEU in TRISO form. General Atomics plans uranium zirconium hydride. Jeff Waksman, the Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Installations, Energy and Environment, leads the effort on the Army side.
The Army frames Janus as energy independence.
A 1 MW to 20 MW generator that runs for years without refueling is a microgrid asset, not a power plant. Diesel gensets and batteries carry most installations through an outage today. Both depend on fuel deliveries or on a short discharge window. A reactor sized to a base changes the resilience math, because the fuel is already on site.
They do not speed up the licensing.
Milestone-based payment protects the money, not the timeline. If Antares, BWXT, General Atomics, Radiant and Westinghouse all slip together, the Army has spent little and gained nothing on schedule. The resilience claim needs a test as well.

European Strategic Autonomy Is an Illusion
European countries possess few aircraft capable of collecting signals intelligence (SIGINT) and electronic intelligence (ELINT); most of their aircraft that have these capabilities are American-made.
Moreover, the countries that operate the largest proportion of these platforms—Turkey and the United Kingdom—are members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) but not of the European Union (EU).
Europe also lacks high-end kinetic combat and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) drones.
Currently, the European drone market is dominated by General Atomics, a U.S. company, while Turkey is the continent’s newest major drone supplier. NATO is also heavily dependent on the United States for space assets.
At the same time, Washington provides the alliance with the majority of its large tanker and transport fleets for aerial refueling and strategic air mobility. These deficiencies in strategic enablers leave Europe with a dearth of sovereign military action capabilities.
The European Commission’s most recent defense assessment, the Joint White Paper for European Defense Readiness 2030, lists seven capability gaps it must close: space assets, air and missile defense, cyber and electronic warfare, drones and anti-drone systems, military mobility, artillery systems, and strategic enablers.
